title: Unless, As Long As and Provided
summary: Describe an exception with unless and set conditions with as long as, so long as, provided and providing. Keep the difference between an exception and a requirement clear, especially in plans about the future.
learningObjectives: Explain unless as except if and use it to identify the exception to a general plan, rule or prediction.
Rephrase simple negative conditions with unless without reversing the intended meaning.
Express permission or agreement that depends on a requirement using as long as or so long as.
Use provided (that) and providing (that) for explicit conditions, including more formal instructions.
Use present forms rather than future will inside these conditional clauses when referring to future possibilities.

explanation.heading: Unless identifies an exception
explanation.body: Unless means except if. A statement with unless usually describes what will happen in general, with one possible situation that would change it. For example, a plan to travel will go ahead except if a specified problem occurs. Read the main clause first, then ask what event would prevent or change it. Unless does not mean the same as because or until.
explanation.example: We will hold the outdoor lesson unless the forecast changes.

explanation.heading: Understand negative statements with unless
explanation.body: In negative main clauses, unless often means that an action will not happen except under one condition. It may be possible to paraphrase the idea with if ... not, but be careful not to add a second negative or reverse the meaning. Not unless is also a short response meaning only if a specified condition is met. In imagined situations, a past form can follow unless.
explanation.example: The receptionist will not release the parcel unless you show identification.

explanation.heading: As long as and so long as set requirements
explanation.body: As long as and so long as introduce a condition that must be satisfied for something to be allowed, accepted or true. The focus is on the requirement, rather than an exception to a normal plan. These expressions are common when making agreements, offering help and granting permission. In this sense, as long as is not about the length of time.
explanation.example: You can work in the studio as long as you clean your desk afterwards.

explanation.heading: Provided and providing introduce conditions
explanation.body: Provided (that) and providing (that) mean on condition that. The word that is optional, and both provided and providing can introduce the requirement. Provided that can sound more formal than as long as, so it fits rules, offers and practical arrangements. Do not add of after provided.
explanation.example: The organiser will extend the deadline provided that every participant agrees.

explanation.heading: Future results, present-tense conditions
explanation.body: A future result can use will, but its unless, as long as, so long as, provided or providing clause normally uses the present simple to describe a possible future event. Say unless the delivery arrives, not unless the delivery will arrive. The same pattern applies to agreements such as we will start as long as everyone is ready. The present form does not mean the condition is happening now.
explanation.example: We will book the room providing there are enough volunteers by Friday.

left.label: Unless: exception
left.example: We will walk to the venue unless it rains.
left.note: Walking is the default plan; rain is the possible reason for changing it.

right.label: As long as: requirement
right.example: We will walk to the venue as long as the path is safe.
right.note: Walking depends on the condition that the path is safe.

left.label: Unless
left.example: You cannot join the rehearsal unless you register.
left.note: The only possible exception to the restriction is registration.

right.label: Only if
right.example: You can join the rehearsal only if you register.
right.note: This highlights the same necessary condition from a positive starting point.

left.label: As long as
left.example: You may borrow the tripod as long as you return it tonight.
left.note: Natural for a personal agreement with a clear requirement.

right.label: Provided that
right.example: Equipment may be borrowed provided that it is returned tonight.
right.note: The condition is explicit and fits a formal lending policy.

examples.sentence: Unless the power fails, the evening class will finish at nine.
examples.note: The class is expected to finish normally, with a power failure as the exception.

examples.sentence: I will not share the draft unless the author gives permission.
examples.note: The negative main clause states a restriction and the condition that would lift it.

examples.sentence: You can keep the spare key as long as you tell us when you return it.
examples.note: As long as introduces the requirement attached to permission.

examples.sentence: Providing everyone brings a ticket, the group can enter together.
examples.note: Providing introduces the condition needed for the group plan.

examples.sentence: The repair will be free provided that the damage is covered by the warranty.
examples.note: Provided that states a requirement in a policy-like context.

examples.sentence: We would not change the schedule unless a serious problem arose.
examples.note: Unless can introduce a past-form condition in a hypothetical situation.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We will continue the trip unless it will rain.
commonMistakes.correct: We will continue the trip unless it rains.
commonMistakes.why: Use a present tense rather than will inside an unless-clause referring to a possible future event.

commonMistakes.incorrect: You may use my laptop as long you handle it carefully.
commonMistakes.correct: You may use my laptop as long as you handle it carefully.
commonMistakes.why: The conditional expression is as long as; both occurrences of as are required.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The offer is valid provided of you reply today.
commonMistakes.correct: The offer is valid provided you reply today.
commonMistakes.why: Provided introduces the condition directly; it does not take of.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Unless you do not sign the form, you cannot take part.
commonMistakes.correct: Unless you sign the form, you cannot take part.
commonMistakes.why: The intended requirement is to sign. With cannot in the main clause, adding not after unless reverses the condition.

studyTips: Paraphrase an unless-rule as an only-if rule and verify that permission or restriction has not changed.
For each agreement, identify the required action, then practise both as long as and provided that without changing the condition.
When a sentence predicts the future, check the verb immediately after unless or provided: use a present form rather than will.

exercises.prompt: The rehearsal is scheduled for tonight. It will be cancelled only if the lead singer becomes ill. Which statement preserves that meaning?
choices: The rehearsal will be cancelled as long as the singer becomes ill.
The rehearsal will go ahead unless the singer becomes ill.
The rehearsal will go ahead provided the singer becomes ill.
exercises.feedback: Unless identifies the possible illness as an exception to the plan to hold the rehearsal.

exercises.prompt: A neighbour can borrow your ladder, but they must bring it back before dark. Choose the natural conditional offer.
choices: You may borrow my ladder as long as you return it before dark.
You may borrow my ladder unless you return it before dark.
You may borrow my ladder because you return it before dark.
exercises.feedback: As long as introduces the requirement the borrower must meet.

exercises.prompt: A policy says the company will pay for training only if a manager approves it. Choose the formal conditional statement.
choices: The company will pay for training provided of a manager approves it.
The company will pay for training provided a manager will approve it.
The company will pay for training provided that a manager approves it.
exercises.feedback: Provided that introduces a condition directly, and approves is present simple for the future requirement.

exercises.prompt: You intend to cycle home, except if the weather gets worse. Which is correct?
choices: I will cycle home unless the weather gets worse.
I will cycle home as long as the weather gets worse.
I will cycle home unless the weather will get worse.
exercises.feedback: Unless expresses the possible exception; gets rather than will get belongs in the condition.

exercises.prompt: The theatre will open as scheduled ___ the heating breaks down. (one word meaning except if)
acceptedAnswers: unless
exercises.feedback: Unless gives the exceptional event that could change the normal opening plan.

exercises.prompt: You can use my desk ___ ___ ___ you leave it tidy. (write the three-word expression meaning on condition that)
acceptedAnswers: as long as
so long as
exercises.feedback: As long as and so long as both introduce a requirement for permission.

exercises.prompt: The event will go ahead provided that the venue ___ (remain) available. (present simple, third-person singular)
acceptedAnswers: remains
exercises.feedback: Use remains, not will remain, in the conditional clause about a future event.

exercises.prompt: You cannot use the shared account ___ you have authorisation. (use one word meaning except if)
acceptedAnswers: unless
exercises.feedback: The restriction applies except when the person has authorisation.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the future verb in the condition: I will lend you the camera as long as you will return it tonight.
acceptedAnswers: I will lend you the camera as long as you return it tonight.
exercises.feedback: The requirement takes present simple return, even though the lending happens in the future.

exercises.prompt: Correct the subject-verb agreement in the unless-clause: Visitors cannot enter unless they has a pass.
acceptedAnswers: Visitors cannot enter unless they have a pass.
exercises.feedback: They requires have, not has. A pass is the condition for entry.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the conditional expression: You may take part provided of you complete the training.
acceptedAnswers: You may take part provided you complete the training.
exercises.feedback: Provided connects directly to its clause; there is no of.

exercises.prompt: Correct the missing verb in the exception clause: The concert will go ahead unless the weather bad.
acceptedAnswers: The concert will go ahead unless the weather is bad.
exercises.feedback: Unless must introduce a grammatical clause; the singular subject the weather needs the verb is before bad.

speakingExercises.prompt: A visitor needs a ticket to enter. State the restriction in one sentence beginning "You cannot enter" and using "unless you have a ticket".
acceptedAnswers: You cannot enter unless you have a ticket.
You can't enter unless you have a ticket.
speakingExercises.feedback: Unless introduces the condition that would allow entry.

speakingExercises.prompt: Offer your bicycle on one condition: the friend returns it by five. Begin "You can borrow my bicycle" and use "as long as".
acceptedAnswers: You can borrow my bicycle as long as you return it by five.
speakingExercises.feedback: As long as states what the borrower must do.

speakingExercises.prompt: The report will be published only if the editor approves it. Begin "The report will be published" and use "provided that".
acceptedAnswers: The report will be published provided that the editor approves it.
speakingExercises.feedback: Provided that introduces the condition, with present-simple approves.

speakingExercises.prompt: You plan to have lunch outdoors, except if the wind gets stronger. Begin "We will eat outside" and use "unless".
acceptedAnswers: We will eat outside unless the wind gets stronger.
We'll eat outside unless the wind gets stronger.
speakingExercises.feedback: The stronger wind is the event that would change the planned lunch.

speakingExercises.prompt: Convert the permission into a restriction. Original: "You may join only if you register." Begin "You cannot join" and use "unless".
acceptedAnswers: You cannot join unless you register.
You can't join unless you register.
speakingExercises.feedback: You cannot join unless you register states the same necessary condition.

speakingExercises.prompt: Explain a hypothetical reaction. Facts: Olivia would complain only if the food was cold. Begin "Olivia would not complain" and end with "unless the food was cold".
acceptedAnswers: Olivia would not complain unless the food was cold.
Olivia wouldn't complain unless the food was cold.
speakingExercises.feedback: Unless can introduce a past-form condition in a hypothetical situation.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences about workshop access. First: visitors cannot enter without signing in; begin "Visitors cannot enter" and use "unless". Second: visitors may stay if they wear a badge; begin "They can stay" and use "as long as".
acceptedAnswers: Visitors cannot enter unless they sign in. They can stay as long as they wear a badge.
Visitors can't enter unless they sign in. They can stay as long as they wear a badge.
speakingExercises.feedback: The first sentence states an exception to a restriction; the second states a continuing condition.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences about tomorrow. First: the team will practise unless the hall is closed; begin "The team will practise". Second: the coach will help on condition that everyone arrives by nine; begin "The coach will help" and use "provided" without that.
acceptedAnswers: The team will practise unless the hall is closed. The coach will help provided everyone arrives by nine.
The team will practice unless the hall is closed. The coach will help provided everyone arrives by nine.
speakingExercises.feedback: Unless supplies an exception to the plan; provided introduces the attendance requirement.

listeningExercises.audioText: The ferry will not leave unless the fog clears, and it is still difficult to see the harbour.
listeningExercises.prompt: What must happen before the ferry can leave?
choices: The fog must become thicker.
The fog must clear.
The ferry must return to the dock.
listeningExercises.feedback: The ferry will not leave unless the fog clears, so clearing fog is required for departure.

listeningExercises.audioText: You can use the practice room as long as you return the key before six this evening.
listeningExercises.prompt: What condition does the speaker set for using the practice room?
choices: The user must return the key by six.
The user must arrive at six.
The user must bring their own instrument.
listeningExercises.feedback: As long as introduces the key-return deadline as the condition for permission.

listeningExercises.audioText: The walking tour will go ahead unless the guide is ill tomorrow.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single conditional word immediately after "ahead" in the audio.
acceptedAnswers: unless
listeningExercises.feedback: Unless introduces the one event that would stop the planned tour.

listeningExercises.audioText: We can extend the deadline by two days provided that everyone on the team agrees.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the plan to extend the deadline depend on?
choices: The meeting ending early.
A manager cancelling the task.
Every team member agreeing.
listeningExercises.feedback: Provided that introduces the agreement as a necessary condition.

listeningExercises.audioText: I will meet you outside the station unless my appointment runs late.
listeningExercises.prompt: When would the speaker change the plan to meet outside?
choices: If the appointment runs late.
If the appointment ends early.
If the other person arrives first.
listeningExercises.feedback: Unless identifies an appointment running late as the exception to meeting outside.

listeningExercises.audioText: Visitors may enter the laboratory providing they sign the safety register first.
listeningExercises.prompt: What must visitors do before entering the laboratory?
choices: Wait until the following day.
Sign the safety register.
Pay a small entrance fee.
listeningExercises.feedback: Providing introduces the required safety registration before access.

listeningExercises.audioText: The loan will be approved as long as the application is complete.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word expression heard immediately after "approved".
acceptedAnswers: as long as
listeningExercises.feedback: The audible phrase as long as introduces a condition for approval.

listeningExercises.audioText: We will set up the market stalls providing the weather stays dry.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single word heard immediately after "stalls".
acceptedAnswers: providing
listeningExercises.feedback: Providing introduces the condition that the weather remain dry.
